days.title: Responsible AI: Six Principles, Guardrails, and Harm Mitigation

concepts.heading: Fairness and Reliability and Safety
concepts.body: Microsoft describes six principles for responsible AI, and the exam usually gives you a short story and asks which principle is at stake. Fairness means an AI system treats all people fairly and does not give different outcomes to similar people because of the group they belong to. For example, a hiring model trained on years of biased past decisions ranks women lower than men with the same skills; it has learned the bias in its training data. To check fairness, compare error rates and outcomes across groups instead of trusting one overall accuracy score. Reliability and safety means the system works as designed, behaves safely in unexpected conditions and resists harmful manipulation. A drone model that finds turbine cracks in clear weather but misses them in fog, which was rare in its training data, is a reliability and safety problem: test across the full range of real conditions before release.

concepts.heading: Privacy and Security and Inclusiveness
concepts.body: Privacy and security means AI systems protect personal data and resist attacks. Typical measures are removing personal data the task does not need, limiting who can read logs and conversations, and encrypting stored data, with a customer-managed key when policy requires the organization to control the keys. For example, a bank that transcribes support calls can run PII detection in Azure Language in Foundry Tools to redact names and card numbers before analysts or a model see the text. Microsoft also states that prompts sent to Foundry Models sold by Azure are not shared with OpenAI and are not used to train foundation models without the customer's permission. Inclusiveness means designing AI so people with different abilities and circumstances can all use it. A bus delay app that explains everything with colored maps fails blind users; adding text and speech alternatives and testing with a diverse range of people applies inclusiveness.

concepts.heading: Transparency and Accountability
concepts.body: Transparency means people understand how an AI system works, what it can and cannot do, and when they are dealing with AI. Two common exam forms are interpretability, such as telling a declined loan applicant which factors most influenced the decision, and disclosure, such as telling listeners that an audiobook narrator is a synthetic voice or making a chatbot say it is an AI. Microsoft publishes Transparency Notes that describe how a service works, its capabilities and limitations, and the choices that affect its behavior. Accountability means the people and organizations that design and deploy AI remain answerable for it. AI should not be the final authority on decisions that affect people's lives, and humans keep meaningful control over highly autonomous systems. Using a model from the Foundry model catalog does not move accountability to the provider: the company that builds the app owns it, with named owners, approvals and records of who deployed which model and when.

concepts.heading: Identify, Measure, Mitigate, Operate
concepts.body: Microsoft's guidance for generative AI follows four stages taken from its Responsible AI Standard. Identify potential harms and prioritize them, for example through red teaming, where testers deliberately try to make the system produce harmful, false or off-policy answers. Measure how often and how severely those harms occur, with clear metrics, test sets and repeated manual and automated testing. Mitigate the harms with tools such as prompt engineering and guardrails, then measure again to see whether the mitigation worked. Operate the system with a deployment and operational readiness plan: phased delivery to a limited group first, an incident response and rollback plan, feedback channels and monitoring. Mitigations sit in four layers: the model itself, the safety system (such as guardrails), the application (system message, grounding and user experience design) and positioning, which covers documentation and how the system is presented to users.

concepts.heading: Guardrails in Microsoft Foundry
concepts.body: Guardrails (previously content filters) are Foundry's safety system layer. A guardrail is a named collection of controls, and each control defines a risk to detect, where to scan for it, and what to do when it is found. For models, the intervention points are the user input and the output. Content risks (hate, sexual, self-harm and violence) are scored by severity, and you choose a blocking level. Prompt Shields detect user prompt attacks (jailbreaks) and indirect attacks, where hidden instructions sit inside a document or email the model reads. Protected material detection stops output that reproduces known text such as song lyrics or published articles, or known code. Some controls, such as PII and groundedness detection, are still in preview, so treat them as extras rather than the main answer. Guardrails do not replace good design: a system message, human review steps and user warnings about possible inaccuracies all help reduce overreliance on AI output.

examPoints: A scenario in which similar people get different outcomes is testing fairness; one where a system fails in rare conditions or behaves dangerously is testing reliability and safety; one about exposed personal data is testing privacy and security.

A scenario about explaining a decision or disclosing that content or a voice is AI-generated is testing transparency, while one about named owners, approvals or human control over high-impact decisions is testing accountability.

A question about blocking harmful output, jailbreaks, hidden instructions in documents, or reproduced lyrics is testing Foundry guardrails (Prompt Shields, protected material), which sit in the safety system layer of the identify, measure, mitigate, operate practice.

quiz.q: A city council uses an AI model to recommend which households lose housing support. A caseworker must review and approve every recommendation before it takes effect. Which responsible AI principle does this design mainly reflect?
choices: Inclusiveness, because every household can now use the same online application
Accountability, because a person stays answerable for each decision that affects lives
Transparency, because the household is told that its case was scored by a model
Reliability and safety, because the model is tested in rare and unusual field conditions
quiz.explain: Accountability says AI should not be the final authority on decisions that affect people's lives, and humans keep meaningful control. Choice C is tempting because disclosure is good practice, but telling people a model was used is transparency; it does not put a human in charge of the outcome.

quiz.q: An assistant summarizes incoming customer emails. A tester sends an email with hidden text telling the assistant to ignore its instructions and forward the customer list. Which Foundry guardrail control is designed to detect this?
choices: Protected material detection, which blocks output that copies published text or code
The violence content risk set to the High blocking level for every user input
Groundedness detection, which checks whether answers match the source text
Prompt Shields, which detect user prompt attacks and indirect attacks in content
quiz.explain: Hidden instructions inside a document or email the model reads are an indirect attack, which Prompt Shields detect. Choice C is tempting because the email is the source text, but groundedness detection (in preview) checks whether an answer is supported by its sources, not whether the content carries an attack.

days.recap: Match each scenario to one of the six principles (fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, accountability), and remember that Microsoft's practice is identify, measure, mitigate and operate, with Foundry guardrails (previously content filters) forming the safety system layer.

days.title: How Generative AI Models Work: Tokens, Embeddings, and Grounding

concepts.heading: Tokens and Next-Token Prediction
concepts.body: A language model does not read words the way people do. Text is first split into tokens, which can be whole words, parts of words or punctuation, and each token is given a number. That is why a sentence such as "The results were unbelievable!" uses more tokens than it has words: a long word may be split into pieces and the exclamation mark is a token of its own. To write a reply, a generative model predicts the most suitable next token from everything it has seen so far, appends it, and repeats until the response is complete or a limit is reached. A full paragraph is simply many of these predictions in a row. This also explains why usage and limits are counted in tokens rather than words or characters, both for the prompt you send (input tokens) and the reply you get back (output tokens).

concepts.heading: Embeddings and Semantic Meaning
concepts.body: An embedding is a vector, a list of numbers, that represents the meaning of a token, a sentence or a whole document. Models learn embeddings so that items with similar meanings end up close together in that vector space, even when they share no words. For example, an internal help site can match the question "I can't sign in anymore" to an article titled "Recover a forgotten password" by comparing their embeddings with a measure such as cosine similarity. Keyword search would miss this match because the two texts have almost no words in common. Embedding models produce these vectors and are a separate model type from chat models: they return numbers, not text. Search over embeddings is often called vector or semantic search, and it is the retrieval step of most retrieval augmented generation (RAG) solutions, typically with the vectors stored in an index such as Azure AI Search.

concepts.heading: Transformers, Attention, and the Context Window
concepts.body: Modern language models are built on the transformer architecture. Its key idea is attention: when the model processes a token, it weighs the other tokens around it according to how much they influence that token's meaning. In "I heard a dog bark", attention lets the model connect "bark" with "dog" and treat it as a sound, not the bark of a tree. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can consider in one request. It must hold the system message, any grounding data, the conversation history, the new user message and the reply, and for reasoning models also the hidden reasoning tokens. A chat app that keeps sending a growing history will eventually reach the limit, so apps trim old turns while keeping the system message. Long prompts also raise usage, because pay-per-token deployments count input tokens as well as output tokens.

concepts.heading: Training Versus Inference
concepts.body: Training is the process in which a model learns: its internal weights are adjusted from very large amounts of data until it predicts tokens well. Fine-tuning is a further, smaller training run on your own examples that adjusts a copy of the weights. Inference is using a trained model to produce output for a prompt. Every chat request to a deployed model is inference, and the weights stay fixed, so the model does not learn from your conversations. A manager who believes a deployed model is getting smarter from daily employee chats has confused the two. Within one request a model can follow examples you include in the prompt (few-shot examples), but it forgets them as soon as the request ends. If you want new knowledge in answers, you add it to the prompt; if you want lasting changes to behavior or style, you fine-tune.

concepts.heading: Hallucination, Grounding, RAG, and Fine-Tuning
concepts.body: Because a model predicts likely tokens, it can produce fluent, confident text that is wrong, called a hallucination or fabrication. The main remedy is grounding: put trusted data in the prompt and tell the model to answer only from it, cite its sources, and say it does not know when the data has no answer. Retrieval augmented generation automates this: an embedding model finds the passages most related to the question, and a chat model writes an answer grounded in them. RAG fits private or frequently changing knowledge, such as product terms updated every week, because you update the index, not the model, and answers can point to the source. Fine-tuning fits a different need: teaching a model a consistent behavior, tone or output format from many examples, for instance so a smaller model follows a house reply style. A useful rule is RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behavior.

examPoints: A question that says a request used more tokens than words, or that compares input and output usage, is testing tokenization; one that matches texts with no shared words is testing embeddings and vector similarity.
A question that says a deployed model is learning from users' chats is testing training versus inference: chat requests are inference, and only training or fine-tuning changes the weights.

A question about confident but invented answers, or about knowledge that changes weekly, is testing grounding and RAG; one about a consistent style or format learned from many examples is testing fine-tuning.

quiz.q: An insurer wants a chat assistant to answer questions from its policy terms, which legal staff update every week. Each answer must reflect the latest terms and cite the source section. Which approach fits best?
choices: Retrieval augmented generation that searches an index of the current terms for each question
Fine-tuning a chat model every week on the full text of the latest version of the terms
Raising the model's temperature so that it writes more varied and detailed answers to users
Choosing a model with a larger context window and relying on its general knowledge of insurance
quiz.explain: RAG retrieves the current passages at question time and grounds the answer in them, so citations point to the latest terms. Choice B is tempting because it uses the insurer's data, but fine-tuning changes behavior and style, needs a new training run for every update and cannot cite sources reliably.

quiz.q: In the sentence "I heard a dog bark", how does a transformer model work out that "bark" means a sound and not part of a tree?
choices: It looks the word up in a fixed dictionary that stores one meaning for each English word
It counts how many times the word appeared in its training data and picks the commonest sense
Attention weighs the surrounding tokens, such as "dog", when it builds the meaning of "bark"
It sends the sentence to a search engine and copies the definition from the first web result
quiz.explain: Attention lets each token's representation depend on the other tokens that influence it, so "dog" shapes the meaning of "bark". Choice B is tempting because training data frequency matters, but a frequency count alone would give every "bark" the same meaning regardless of context.

days.recap: Models split text into tokens, represent meaning as embeddings, use attention to read context within a limited context window, and write by predicting the next token at inference time; reduce hallucination with grounding and RAG, and use fine-tuning only to change behavior or style.

days.title: Choosing a Model and Configuring a Deployment

concepts.heading: LLMs, SLMs, and Reasoning Models
concepts.body: A large language model (LLM) has many parameters and is trained on huge amounts of data, so it handles broad, open-ended language tasks well, from drafting reports to answering varied questions. A small language model (SLM), such as a model from the Phi family, has fewer parameters. It gives up some top-end reasoning in exchange for faster responses, lower cost and the ability to run on modest or edge hardware. For example, classifying short delivery notes on warehouse scanners with an unreliable network is a good SLM task. Reasoning models are trained to work through a problem step by step before answering, using hidden reasoning tokens that take up context window space and count toward the output limit. Choose one for multi-step math, science, planning or complex problem solving where accuracy matters more than an instant reply, and a standard chat model when quick conversational answers are enough.

concepts.heading: Multimodal, Embedding, and Image Models
concepts.body: Models are also chosen by the kind of input and output they handle. A multimodal model accepts more than one type of input, such as text plus images, and returns text, so a technician can upload a photo of a damaged part and ask what is wrong with it. Some models also take and return audio, which suits voice conversations. An embedding model turns text, and in some cases images, into vectors for semantic search, clustering and RAG retrieval; it never writes an answer. A RAG solution therefore needs two model types: an embedding model to find passages by meaning and a chat model to write the grounded reply. Image generation models do the opposite of image understanding: text goes in and a new image comes out, as with the GPT-image series in Foundry. A quick check is to ask what goes in and what must come out, then pick the model type whose inputs and outputs match.

concepts.heading: The Model Catalog and Benchmarks
concepts.body: Microsoft Foundry's model catalog lists models from Microsoft, OpenAI and other providers. Some are Foundry Models sold directly by Azure, while partner and community models come through Azure Marketplace. Each model has a model card that shows its description, supported inputs and outputs, the deployment options it offers, its license terms and, for many models, benchmark results. Benchmarks and model leaderboards let you compare models before you deploy anything. Quality benchmarks score how well a model answers standard test sets, safety benchmarks show how it handles harmful content, and performance metrics describe speed. For a streaming chat where users must see the reply start quickly, the metric to watch is time to first token; throughput describes how many tokens are produced per second. A sensible process is to shortlist models by capability, compare benchmarks, read the license, and then test the finalists with your own prompts.

concepts.heading: Deployment Types
concepts.body: To use a Foundry Model sold by Azure you create a deployment, and its deployment type decides where prompts are processed and how you pay. Learn's advice is to start most workloads on Global Standard: it bills per token, may process requests in any Azure region, gets new models first and has the broadest availability. Data stored at rest stays in your chosen geography whatever the type. If prompts and responses must stay inside the EU, US or Asia Pacific data zone, choose Data Zone Standard; if they must stay in one Azure geography, choose Standard. Provisioned types (Global, Data Zone and Regional Provisioned) reserve throughput for high, steady volume with predictable latency, and you pay for that capacity even when it is idle. Batch types (Global Batch and Data Zone Batch) process large, non-urgent jobs asynchronously at lower cost, such as labeling millions of reviews overnight. The Developer type exists only to evaluate fine-tuned models.

concepts.heading: Configuration Parameters and the System Message
concepts.body: A deployment is shaped further by the request. The system message sets the model's role, scope, tone, format and fallback rules for the whole conversation, while user messages carry each question. Temperature controls randomness: low values give focused, consistent answers, such as for legal or factual text, and higher values give more varied, creative output. Top_p (nucleus sampling) limits choices to the most probable tokens; Microsoft advises changing temperature or top_p, not both. Max tokens caps the length of the reply, and a finish reason of "length" means that cap cut the answer off. A stop sequence ends generation when the model writes a chosen marker, such as ###, and the marker is not returned. Frequency penalty discourages repeating the same lines and presence penalty nudges the model toward new topics. None of these settings adds knowledge to the model; grounding does that.

examPoints: A scenario that stresses speed, low cost or edge devices for a simple language task points to an SLM; multi-step problems where accuracy beats speed point to a reasoning model; image plus text input needing a text answer points to a multimodal model.

A question that mentions data residency in the EU or US zone points to a Data Zone deployment type, steady high volume with predictable latency to provisioned, overnight non-urgent jobs to batch, and no special need to Global Standard.

A question about replies cut off with finish reason "length", repeated sentences, ending at a marker, or consistent versus creative output is testing max tokens, frequency penalty, stop sequences, and temperature or top_p.

quiz.q: A bank in Germany must keep prompts and responses for its chat model processed only inside the EU. Its traffic is moderate and changes through the day. Which deployment type fits most directly?
choices: Global Standard, because data at rest stays in the geography that the bank chose
Global Batch, because asynchronous jobs are always processed in the deployment region
Regional Provisioned, because reserved capacity suits traffic that changes from hour to hour
Data Zone Standard, because it bills per token and processes data only in the EU zone
quiz.explain: Data Zone Standard keeps inference inside the Microsoft-defined data zone and bills per token, which suits variable traffic. Choice A is tempting because data at rest does stay in the geography, but Global Standard may process prompts in any Azure region, which breaks the rule.

quiz.q: A summarizer returns summaries that stop mid-sentence, and each response reports a finish reason of "length". The source documents fit easily in the context window. What should the developer change?
choices: Lower the temperature so that the model writes shorter and more focused sentences
Raise the maximum output tokens setting so that the full summary can be returned
Add a stop sequence so that the model knows where each summary should come to an end
Switch to a Global Batch deployment so that longer jobs can run without any limits
quiz.explain: A finish reason of "length" means the reply hit the output token cap, so raising max tokens (or asking for shorter output) fixes it. Choice C is tempting because it is about where text ends, but a stop sequence ends output earlier at a marker; it cannot extend a reply that was cut off.

days.recap: Pick a model by task and modality (LLM, SLM, reasoning, multimodal, embedding, image generation), compare candidates with model cards and benchmarks, start deployments on Global Standard unless residency, steady volume or batch needs say otherwise, and tune output with the system message, temperature or top_p, max tokens, stop sequences and penalties.

days.title: AI Workloads I: Generative and Agentic AI and Text Analysis

concepts.heading: Recognizing Common AI Workloads
concepts.body: Many exam questions describe a business need and ask which AI workload it is. Decide by looking at the input and the desired output. Generative AI creates new content, such as text, code or images, from a prompt: a first-draft product description that a copywriter then edits is generative AI. Text analysis, also called natural language processing, finds information in text that already exists, such as topics, opinions or names in survey answers. Speech workloads turn audio into text or text into audio. Computer vision recognizes or locates what is in images and video, such as cars in parking bays. Information extraction pulls specific fields from documents, images, audio or video into structured data, such as the shipper and gross weight from scanned bills of lading. Real solutions often combine workloads; a phone-call satisfaction tracker, for example, chains speech recognition with sentiment analysis.

concepts.heading: Generative AI Versus Agentic AI
concepts.body: An AI agent is a generative model plus instructions plus tools. The instructions describe its role and limits, and the tools let it look up live data and take actions in other systems, such as querying a database, booking an appointment or sending an email. A chat app that only answers questions about travel destinations is generative AI; it becomes an agent when it can, for example, check flight availability and make a booking. The test is whether the solution reasons about a goal and then acts through tools, not whether it talks fluently. For example, an insurance assistant that reads a claim message, looks up the policy, books a repair slot in the garage system and emails a confirmation is agentic AI. In Microsoft Foundry, agents are built and run with Foundry Agent Service, which keeps each conversation's history so the agent can handle multi-turn tasks. A voice concierge that books tables combines speech with agentic AI.

concepts.heading: Key Phrases, Entities, and PII
concepts.body: Azure Language in Foundry Tools offers prebuilt text analysis features that return structured, repeatable results. Key phrase extraction returns the main talking points of a text as a short list, such as "login page" and "password reset email" from a bug report. Named entity recognition (NER) finds mentions of people, places, organizations, dates, quantities and more, and labels each with its category. When you need categories the prebuilt model lacks, such as tariff codes, custom NER learns them from labeled examples. PII detection finds personal data such as names, addresses and phone numbers, returns each category with a confidence score, and can return a redacted copy of the text. Use it when results must be predictable and auditable, for example before publishing complaints as open data, rather than asking a generative model to remove personal details in free form. Text analytics for health finds medical entities in clinical text.

concepts.heading: Sentiment, Opinion Mining, and Summarization
concepts.body: Sentiment analysis labels each sentence and the whole document as positive, negative or neutral, with confidence scores for the three labels that add up to 1. A document with both clearly positive and clearly negative sentences, such as "The breakfast was wonderful. The air conditioning was broken all week.", gets the document label mixed. Opinion mining goes further and links each opinion to its target: in "The pasta was excellent, but the waiter was rude" it reports pasta as positive and waiter as negative. Summarization comes in two styles. Extractive summarization returns the most important sentences copied word for word, with their positions in the source, which suits legal staff who must quote a ruling exactly. Abstractive summarization writes new, fluent sentences, which suits a plain-language paragraph for a website. Conversation summarization recaps a chat or call transcript, including the issue and how it was resolved.

concepts.heading: Language Detection and Feature Status
concepts.body: Language detection identifies the language a text is written in and returns its name, an ISO code and a confidence score. It is often the first step of a pipeline, for example to route support tickets to the team that speaks the language before any other processing. Very short or ambiguous inputs, such as the single word "communication", can be detected wrongly; a country hint helps, because the default hint is the US. Azure Language now splits its features into two groups. Core capabilities, recommended for new development, are PII detection, language detection, named entity recognition (prebuilt and custom) and text analytics for health. Key phrase extraction, sentiment analysis and opinion mining, and summarization are legacy capabilities: still supported for existing implementations, but not the focus of new investment. For flexible or combined text tasks without training data, a prompted generative model in Foundry is the alternative.

examPoints: A scenario in which an AI solution looks up data and takes actions in other systems, such as booking or emailing, is agentic AI; one that only writes or answers from a prompt is generative AI.

A request for main talking points is key phrase extraction, for tagged people, places and dates is NER, for names and phone numbers to remove is PII detection, and for which language a text is in is language detection.

A request for positive, negative or neutral labels is sentiment analysis, for the aspect each opinion targets is opinion mining, and for quoted versus newly worded summaries is extractive versus abstractive summarization.

quiz.q: A logistics company is reviewing AI project ideas. Which one is an agentic AI workload rather than generative AI or text analysis?
choices: A model that writes a weekly newsletter draft from a list of bullet points that staff type in
A service that labels each driver's written feedback as positive, negative or neutral
An assistant that checks a truck's live location, reschedules the delivery and texts the customer
A tool that pulls city names and delivery dates out of incoming emails and tags each one by its type
quiz.explain: The assistant reasons about the goal and uses tools to read live data and act in other systems, which makes it an agent. Choice A is tempting because it uses a generative model, but writing a draft from a prompt without taking any action is generative AI.

quiz.q: A hotel group wants to know which part of its service each opinion in a review refers to, for example that the pool was praised while check-in was criticized. Which technique fits?
choices: Opinion mining, which links each opinion to its target and gives that target a sentiment
Key phrase extraction, which returns the main talking points of each review as a list
Document-level sentiment analysis, which gives each review one overall label and score
Extractive summarization, which returns the most important review sentences word for word
quiz.explain: Opinion mining returns targets such as pool and check-in, each with its own assessment and sentiment. Choice C is tempting because it measures sentiment, but a single document label (here likely mixed) cannot say which aspect was praised and which was criticized.

days.recap: Classify workloads by input and output, call a solution agentic only when a model uses tools to act, and map text needs to key phrases, NER, PII detection, sentiment and opinion mining, summarization or language detection, remembering that Azure Language marks PII, language detection and NER as core and key phrases, sentiment and summarization as legacy.

days.title: AI Workloads II: Speech, Vision, Image Generation, and Information Extraction
services: Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools

concepts.heading: Speech Recognition and Speech Synthesis
concepts.body: Speech recognition (speech to text) turns spoken audio into text; speech synthesis (text to speech) turns text into spoken audio. Always check the direction: audio in and text out is recognition, text in and audio out is synthesis. Azure Speech in Foundry Tools offers three ways to transcribe. Real-time transcription handles streaming audio, such as live captions; fast transcription handles single recorded files quickly; batch transcription processes large volumes of stored audio asynchronously, such as all of yesterday's call recordings. If the base model misses industry jargon, a custom speech model trained on domain text and transcribed audio improves accuracy. Diarization labels who said what in a transcript. For synthesis, neural voices use deep neural networks to sound humanlike, and Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) controls pronunciation, pace, pitch and pauses. Custom voice is a Limited Access feature that needs approval and a consenting voice talent.

concepts.heading: Speech Translation and Voice Conversations
concepts.body: Speech translation takes live speech in one language and produces text or speech in one or more other languages, for example showing a presenter's English talk as Spanish and Japanese captions. Plain speech to text and diarization never change the language, and language identification only tells you which language is being spoken. For voice assistants there are two broad designs. A pipeline chains speech to text, a language model and text to speech, which gives you control over voices, SSML and custom recognition. A speech-in, speech-out model, such as gpt-realtime through the Realtime API, hears the audio directly and answers in speech with low latency. Azure Speech also offers Voice Live, which provides fast, natural, interruptible conversations between a person and an agent without managing those pieces yourself. In each case the workload is still speech; it becomes agentic only when the assistant uses tools to act.

concepts.heading: Computer Vision Techniques
concepts.body: Computer vision interprets images and video. Image classification gives one label for the whole image, such as "damaged" or "undamaged". Object detection finds several objects and returns a label and a bounding box for each, such as every car in a car park. Semantic segmentation classifies each pixel, so it gives exact shapes and areas rather than rectangles. Captioning writes a sentence that describes an image, tagging returns searchable keywords, and optical character recognition (OCR) reads printed or handwritten text such as street signs, labels or forms. Face detection, which finds faces and their location, is available to all customers, while face identification (who is this) and verification (are these the same person) are Limited Access features. Microsoft retired facial analysis that infers emotion and gender. Note that Image Analysis in Azure Vision is deprecated and retires on September 25, 2028; for new open-ended image questions, Learn points to multimodal GPT models in Foundry or Content Understanding.

concepts.heading: Multimodal Models and Image Generation
concepts.body: A vision-enabled multimodal model accepts an image together with a text prompt and returns text, so it can describe a chart, answer a question about a photo or read text in a screenshot. It works best when the prompt states the task and context, and it is not meant for medical diagnosis or exact counting where precise numbers matter. Image generation runs the other way: text goes in and a new image comes out. Most modern image generators use diffusion, which starts from random noise and removes it step by step, comparing the result with the prompt until the picture matches the description. In Microsoft Foundry, image generation and editing use the GPT-image series; GPT-image-2 is generally available, and the older DALL-E 3 model has been retired. Editing changes part of an existing image with a prompt and optionally a mask. Prompts and generated images both pass through content moderation, so a harmful request returns no image.

concepts.heading: Extracting Information with Content Understanding
concepts.body: Information extraction turns unstructured content into structured data. OCR alone gives you the text of a page; extraction gives you named fields, such as invoice number, total and due date, ready for a database. Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools handles documents, images, audio and video with analyzers. Prebuilt analyzers cover common cases such as invoices or call center recordings, and custom analyzers use a field schema you define. Each field uses one method: extract copies a value that appears in the content (documents only), classify picks one value from a set of categories, and generate writes a value such as a summary. For documents, confidence scores show how much to trust each value, so only doubtful ones go to a person, and grounding shows where on the page each value came from. For audio and video it first transcribes speech and, for video, splits scenes and key frames, giving timestamped, searchable insights.

examPoints: A question that turns audio into text is speech recognition (real-time for live captions, batch for large stored volumes), text into audio is speech synthesis with SSML for pronunciation and pauses, and speech in one language into another is speech translation.

One label per image is classification, labeled boxes are object detection, pixel outlines are segmentation, and words in an image are OCR; face identification and verification are Limited Access, and emotion and gender inference are retired.

A question that needs named fields, confidence scores or source locations from documents, or timestamped insights from audio and video, is testing information extraction with Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools; text in and a new picture out is image generation.

quiz.q: An insurance company stores thousands of recorded customer calls each day. Every night it wants transcripts of all of them so analysts can search them the next morning. Which Azure Speech capability fits best?
choices: Real-time transcription, which converts each call into text while the customer is speaking
Batch transcription, which processes large volumes of stored audio files asynchronously
Text to speech with SSML, which controls how each recorded call is spoken back to analysts
Speech translation, which turns each recorded call into text written in a second language
quiz.explain: Batch transcription is built for large volumes of stored audio when results can wait. Choice A is tempting because it also produces transcripts, but real-time transcription is meant for streaming audio while people speak, not for overnight processing of recordings.

quiz.q: A freight company receives scanned shipping documents and needs the shipper, consignee and gross weight written into its database, with low-confidence values sent to a clerk. What should it use?
choices: Image classification, which gives each scanned page one label that describes its type
Speech to text, which converts the contents of each document into a searchable transcript
Image generation, which creates a cleaner version of each scan so people can read it easily
A Content Understanding analyzer, which returns schema fields with confidence scores
quiz.explain: A Content Understanding analyzer extracts named fields against a schema and adds confidence scores and grounding so doubtful values can be routed to a person. Choice A is tempting because it works on the scanned pages, but a single label for each page gives no field values at all.

days.recap: Speech recognition and synthesis move between audio and text (with batch, real-time, SSML and translation options), computer vision classifies, detects, segments, captions and reads images (with Face recognition under Limited Access), GPT-image models generate images, and Azure Content Understanding turns documents, images, audio and video into structured fields.

days.title: Prompts and the Foundry Portal

concepts.heading: Foundry Resources, Projects, and the Model Catalog
concepts.body: Microsoft Foundry (formerly Azure AI Foundry) is where you build generative AI apps and agents in Azure. Two pieces matter first. A Foundry resource is the Azure resource that holds model deployments, endpoints and keys, and a Foundry project is a workspace managed under that resource where you build and test. The model catalog lists the models you can deploy, from Azure OpenAI models to partner and community models such as Meta Llama. Each model has a model card that describes what it does. Models sold by Azure, such as the Azure OpenAI models, deploy straight away; partner and community models first need an Azure Marketplace subscription, so the person deploying needs permission to create one. For example, a student who wants to try a Llama model and gets a Marketplace error needs that subscription permission, not a new project. On the exam, the catalog is where you choose and inspect a model, and the resource and project are what you need before you can deploy one.

concepts.heading: Deploying a Model and the Deployment Name
concepts.body: A model in the catalog does nothing until you deploy it. In the Foundry portal you select the model, then Deploy with default settings or with custom settings. One setting deserves attention: the deployment name. By default it matches the model name, but you can change it, and during inference the deployment name is what goes in the model parameter to route a request to that deployment. Deployments also use quota, measured in tokens per minute (TPM) per model and per region; when you run out you request more or move TPM from another deployment of the same model. Your project and resource must be in a region where the model is offered. For example, if a team deploys gpt-4.1-mini under the name support-bot, its code must send support-bot, not gpt-4.1-mini. When the deployment finishes, Foundry opens the model playground so you can try it at once. Exam stems often hide a failure behind a wrong deployment name or a region where the model is not available.

concepts.heading: System Messages and User Messages
concepts.body: A chat model receives a list of messages with roles. The system message comes first and acts as the highest-level set of instructions: the assistant's role, its scope, its tone, the output format, and what it should do when it lacks information or a request is out of scope. User messages carry what the person asks on each turn, and assistant messages are the model's earlier replies. A simple rule helps: anything that stays the same on every call belongs in the system message, and anything that changes on every call belongs in the user message. For example, a bookshop assistant could have the system message 'You recommend books from our shop only. Answer in two sentences. If you don't know, say so.' while the user message is 'Something like The Hobbit for a 10-year-old?'. Learn stresses that a system message steers the model but doesn't guarantee compliance, so you test it with realistic and adversarial prompts and layer it with guardrails and evaluation.

concepts.heading: Few-Shot Examples, Output Format, and Grounding
concepts.body: Several prompt techniques appear on the exam. Few-shot learning means adding example input and output pairs, written as user and assistant messages after the system message, so the model copies the pattern. The model is not permanently changed; the examples only condition that one request, and a prompt with no examples is called zero-shot. If code will parse the reply, state the exact output format, for example 'Return only JSON with the keys name, company and phone_number'. To reduce made-up answers, ground the model by putting the facts it should use into the prompt, such as a short product list in the system message with the rule 'Answer only from this context; if the answer isn't there, say I don't know'. That rule gives the model an 'out'. Large or changing data is better retrieved at question time, for example with Azure AI Search. Because models show recency bias, repeating the key instruction after a long document, or ending with a cue such as 'Key points:', also helps.

concepts.heading: Testing in the Playground: Settings, Compare, Guardrails, and Code
concepts.body: The model playground lets you tune a deployment without writing code. You edit the system message, change parameters such as temperature, top_p and max_tokens, and add tools. A lower temperature gives focused, consistent answers and a higher one gives more variety; Microsoft suggests changing temperature or top_p, not both. Compare mode runs up to three deployed models side by side, each receiving the same prompt, system message and settings, so you can judge quality and speed fairly. Safety is handled by guardrails (previously called content filters), named sets of controls assigned to a model deployment; by default a model gets the Microsoft.DefaultV2 guardrail, and the controls in a guardrail can check user input and model output for risks such as hate, sexual content, violence, self-harm and prompt attacks. When the prompt works, the Code tab shows a ready-to-run sample with your endpoint and deployment name, so the portal experiment becomes the first version of your app.

examPoints: A question that asks where to put an assistant's role, tone, limits or output format is testing the system message; the input that changes on every call goes in the user message.

A question about making a model copy a pattern from a few examples is testing few-shot prompting, while one about stopping invented answers is testing grounding in the prompt with an explicit 'say I don't know' rule.
A question about trying several deployed models on the same prompt is testing compare mode in the model playground, and one about moving a working prompt into an app is testing the Code tab sample.

quiz.q: A help desk app must always reply in JSON with the keys category and urgency, whatever the user writes. Where should the developer state this requirement?
choices: In the guardrail assigned to the deployment, so filtering rejects replies that aren't JSON
In the system message, as an output rule that applies to every turn of the conversation
In a higher temperature setting, so the model tries more structured ways to answer
In each user's own message, by asking users to request JSON at the end of every question
quiz.explain: Fixed rules such as the output format belong in the system message, which the model receives on every call. Choice A is tempting because guardrails control replies, but guardrails detect harmful content; they don't define an output format.

quiz.q: A developer has deployed two chat models and wants to see how each answers the same prompt, with the same system message and settings, before writing any code. What should she use?
choices: The agents playground, saving each model as an agent and running an evaluation on both
The Code tab of each deployment, running the two samples one after the other on her laptop
A single deployment name shared by both models, switching the model behind it between tests
Compare mode in the model playground, which sends one prompt to both models side by side
quiz.explain: Compare mode runs up to three deployed models in parallel with synced prompts and settings, with no code. Choice B is tempting because the code samples also call the models, but that means writing and running code, which she wants to avoid.

days.recap: A Foundry project under a Foundry resource lets you pick a model from the catalog, deploy it under a deployment name, and shape its behavior with a system message, few-shot examples, a stated output format and grounding, then test it in the playground with compare mode, guardrails and the Code tab.

days.title: A Lightweight Chat Client with the Foundry SDK

concepts.heading: The Project Endpoint and the Two Clients
concepts.body: The Foundry SDK is a thin client over all Foundry project APIs, reached through one project endpoint of the form `https://<resource-name>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project-name>`. In Python it is the azure-ai-projects package. It gives you two clients. The project client, AIProjectClient, handles Foundry-native work such as connections and project settings. The OpenAI-compatible client, returned by `project.get_openai_client()`, calls models, agents and evaluations with OpenAI-style requests. The Learn sample is only a few lines: create `AIProjectClient(endpoint=project_endpoint, credential=DefaultAzureCredential())`, get the OpenAI client, call `responses.create(model="gpt-5-mini", input="...")` and print `response.output_text`. The model argument is your deployment name, so if you named the deployment travel-helper, that is what you pass. A chat client for the exam is just this loop around user input: read a question, send it, show the text that comes back.

concepts.heading: Keys or Microsoft Entra ID
concepts.body: Your app must prove who it is. The Foundry SDK samples use Microsoft Entra ID through `DefaultAzureCredential`, which finds a credential in the environment: your Azure CLI sign-in (`az login`) on a developer machine, or a managed identity when the code runs in Azure. Signing in only identifies the caller; the identity also needs an Azure RBAC role. For day-to-day development the role is Foundry User (formerly Azure AI User) on the project; a caller that only uses agents, without creating them, can have Foundry Agent Consumer. API keys still work on the OpenAI-compatible `/openai/v1` endpoint, but a key grants full access to anyone who holds it. Learn's rule: never put keys in code or a repository, keep them in Azure Key Vault or environment variables, rotate them, and prefer Microsoft Entra ID. For example, a web app in Azure App Service would use its managed identity with the Foundry User role, so no secret is stored anywhere.

concepts.heading: Responses API or Chat Completions
concepts.body: Two APIs can generate a chat reply. The Responses API is the newer one: it brings chat completions and the older Assistants API together, can keep state on the service, and supports the latest features and tools. Learn recommends considering it for new apps, and the Foundry SDK's OpenAI client targets it. You send `input` and read `output_text`; for a follow-up turn you pass `previous_response_id` with the ID of the last response, so you don't resend the history yourself. The Chat Completions API is the older, stateless style: you send a `messages` list with system, user and assistant roles and read `choices[0].message.content`. It remains available for existing apps and for some partner models. For example, a new course-advice chatbot would start on the Responses API, while an older app already built on Chat Completions can keep running and move later. Exam stems that say 'new app' and 'recommended' point to Responses.

concepts.heading: Keeping the Conversation and Watching the Context Window
concepts.body: A model has no memory between calls. With Chat Completions, your code keeps the conversation: it appends each user message and each assistant reply to the messages list and sends the whole list every time, or the model forgets earlier questions. With the Responses API, you chain turns with `previous_response_id` or use a conversation object, and the service can manage the history for you. Either way, the history counts against the model's context window on every request. A long chat eventually reaches the limit, so Learn suggests tracking token counts and removing the oldest user and assistant turns while always keeping the system message, or starting a new conversation. For example, a tutoring bot that loses its 'answer as a patient tutor' style after an hour probably trimmed too much, or the system message was crowded out. On the exam, 'the bot forgets what I said a moment ago' means the history isn't being sent.

concepts.heading: Streaming, finish_reason, and Blocked Requests
concepts.body: A long reply can take several seconds, so a chat client usually streams it: set `stream=True` and show each piece of text as it arrives instead of waiting for the full answer. Every Chat Completions response carries a `finish_reason` that says why the output ended. `stop` means the model finished normally. `length` means the output was cut off by the max_tokens or max_completion_tokens limit or the model's token limit, so you raise the limit or ask for less. `content_filter` means content was left out because a guardrail flagged it, and `tool_calls` means the model wants your app to call a tool. When streaming, finish_reason is null until the last chunk. If the prompt itself is blocked, the call fails with HTTP 400 and the code content_filter, so a good client handles both the blocked prompt and the filtered reply. For example, a summary that stops mid-sentence with finish_reason length needs a higher token limit, not a new model.

examPoints: A question about connecting code to a Foundry project is testing the project endpoint, `AIProjectClient`, `get_openai_client()` and the deployment name passed as model.
A question that says the caller signs in but is refused is testing RBAC: the identity also needs a role such as Foundry User, and Microsoft Entra ID is preferred over keys stored in code.
A question about a bot that forgets earlier turns is testing conversation history, while one about a reply cut off mid-sentence is testing finish_reason length and the output token limit.

quiz.q: A developer's Python app uses DefaultAzureCredential and signs in successfully, but every call to the Foundry project is refused with a permission error. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Replace the project endpoint with the openai.azure.com endpoint of the same resource
Store an API key in the source code next to the endpoint so the call is accepted
Assign the Foundry User role on the project to the identity the app signs in with
Switch the code from the Responses API to the Chat Completions API for the same model
quiz.explain: Signing in proves identity, but the identity also needs an RBAC role such as Foundry User to use the project. Choice B is tempting because a key would bypass the role check, but keys must never sit in code and Microsoft recommends Entra ID.

quiz.q: A study-helper app built on Chat Completions returns summaries that stop in the middle of a sentence. The response shows finish_reason set to length. What should the developer do?
choices: Raise the max_tokens or max_completion_tokens value, or ask the model for a shorter summary
Assign a stricter guardrail to the deployment, because a filter removed the end of the text
Add the previous assistant replies to the messages list, because the model lost its history
Set stream to true, because a streamed reply is never cut off by a token limit or filter
quiz.explain: finish_reason length means the output hit the token limit, so raise it or ask for less. Choice B is tempting because text is missing, but a filtered reply shows finish_reason content_filter, not length.

days.recap: A lightweight chat client connects to the project endpoint with AIProjectClient and Microsoft Entra ID, calls the Responses API (or Chat Completions for existing code) with the deployment name, keeps or chains the conversation within the context window, streams long replies and checks finish_reason.

days.title: Agents in Foundry Agent Service

concepts.heading: What an Agent Is
concepts.body: A plain model call is one request: you send input and get text back. An agent adds a saved definition around the model. In Foundry Agent Service, the simplest kind is a prompt agent, defined by three things: a deployed model, instructions, and optional tools. Foundry stores the agent, runs it for you, and applies its instructions to every response, so there is no code or infrastructure to manage. Instructions play the role of a system message: the agent's job, tone, limits and when to use each tool. Tools let it do more than generate text, such as search your files or run code. For example, an HR agent could use a gpt-4.1-mini deployment, the instructions 'Answer questions about our leave policy only, and cite the policy section', and a file search tool over the policy documents. Before creating an agent you must deploy a model. For the exam: model plus instructions plus tools equals an agent; a model alone is just a model.

concepts.heading: Knowledge and Compute Tools
concepts.body: Three built-in tools come up most often. File search grounds an agent in your own documents: you upload files to a vector store and attach the tool, and the agent retrieves relevant passages before it answers. Code interpreter lets the agent write and run Python in a sandbox, which suits calculations, data files such as CSVs, and charts. Web search lets the agent answer with current public information and inline citations; it uses Grounding with Bing, so the queries leave your compliance boundary and add cost, which matters for confidential questions. The tools combine well: a sales agent might use file search for product sheets and code interpreter to total a CSV of orders exactly, because a model guessing at sums is unreliable. Tools also depend on support: a tool runs only if both the model and the region support it. Recommend the generally available tools, and treat anything marked preview as optional.

concepts.heading: Action Tools: Function Calling and OpenAPI
concepts.body: Some tasks need your own systems. With function calling, you describe a function by name, parameters and description. When the model decides it needs it, the response contains a function call; your app runs the function, then sends the result back as a function_call_output in the same conversation, and the agent finishes its answer. Foundry never runs your function itself. You can run agents that have function tools in the portal, but you add or change function definitions with the SDK or REST API. The OpenAPI tool is different: you give the agent an OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 specification of an existing REST API, each operation with an operationId, and the agent calls the API directly, authenticating anonymously, with an API key through a project connection, or with the project's managed identity. For example, a delivery-status API already described by an OpenAPI spec suits the OpenAPI tool, while a check that runs inside your own app suits a function.

concepts.heading: Testing in the Agents Playground and Agent Versions
concepts.body: The agents playground in the Foundry portal lets you build and test an agent without code. You choose the model, write the instructions, attach tools and knowledge, and chat with the agent over several turns, with tracing to see which tools it called. Agents are named, versioned assets. Once saved, a version can't be changed; each change is saved as a new version, and in code you can refer to `<agent_name>:<version>`. Versions let you compare configurations, send the same inputs to two versions, and roll back. Unsaved changes are temporary: you can try them in the playground, but to view conversation history, compare versions or run full evaluations you must save. For example, if a new instruction makes a support agent worse, you send traffic to the previous version. If an agent ignores a tool, say in its instructions when to use it, and check the trace.

concepts.heading: A Client App: Conversations and Responses
concepts.body: An app talks to an agent through the project endpoint with a Microsoft Entra ID credential and the agent's name. The Learn quickstart creates `AIProjectClient(endpoint, DefaultAzureCredential())`, gets an OpenAI client bound to the agent with `project.get_openai_client(agent_name=...)`, creates a conversation once with `openai.conversations.create()`, then calls `openai.responses.create(conversation=conversation.id, input="...")` for each user turn and reads `output_text`. The conversation holds the history, so reuse its ID for follow-up questions and give each user or topic its own conversation. A new conversation starts with an empty history. The caller needs a role such as Foundry User on the project. This replaces the classic pattern of threads, messages and runs: classic agents are deprecated and retire on March 31, 2027, so new apps use conversations and responses. In short: the agent is the definition, the conversation is the history, a response is one run.

examPoints: A question that contrasts a single model call with a reusable assistant that has instructions and tools is testing what an agent is: model plus instructions plus tools, saved and versioned in Foundry Agent Service.

A question about answering from company files is testing file search, one about exact calculations or charts is testing code interpreter, and one about current web facts is testing web search with its compliance trade-off.

A question about a client that loses history or mixes users is testing conversations: create one per user or chat session, pass its ID on every response, and don't build new apps on classic threads and runs.

quiz.q: An agent must check stock levels by calling a small function that runs inside the company's own app. How does function calling handle this in Foundry Agent Service?
choices: Foundry uploads the function code to a sandbox and runs it with the code interpreter tool
The agent reads the function from a vector store and copies the stock numbers into its answer
The agent calls the function's URL directly, using the project's managed identity to sign in
The model requests the call, and the app runs the function and returns its output to the agent
quiz.explain: With function calling the model only asks for the call; your app executes it and sends back the output. Choice C is tempting because some tools do call APIs directly, but that describes the OpenAPI tool, not a function tool.

quiz.q: A chat app sends each new user question to an agent, but the agent never remembers the user's earlier questions. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The agent has no file search tool, so it can't store what users said in a vector store
The app creates a new conversation for each question instead of reusing the conversation ID
The app uses the agent's name instead of a fixed version number in the client code
The agent's instructions are too long, so Foundry drops the oldest messages after each turn
quiz.explain: History lives in the conversation, so a new conversation per question means an empty history each time. Choice A is tempting because file search stores data, but it grounds answers in uploaded documents; it isn't chat memory.

days.recap: A Foundry agent is a deployed model plus instructions plus tools such as file search, code interpreter, web search, function calling and OpenAPI, tested and versioned in the agents playground and called from an app through conversations and responses, which replace the deprecated classic threads and runs.

days.title: Text and Speech Apps

concepts.heading: Azure Language: Core and Legacy Capabilities
concepts.body: Azure Language in Foundry Tools analyzes text and returns structured results. Learn now splits its features into two groups. Core capabilities are recommended for new development: PII detection, language detection, named entity recognition (prebuilt NER and custom NER), and text analytics for health. Legacy capabilities stay supported for existing workloads: key phrase extraction, sentiment analysis and opinion mining, summarization, entity linking, question answering, conversational language understanding and custom text classification. Each core feature has a clear job. PII detection finds personal data such as names and phone numbers and returns a redacted copy of the text. Language detection returns the language name, its ISO 639-1 code and a confidence score. Prebuilt NER tags people, places, dates and other general types. Text analytics for health extracts medical entities such as medications and dosages. For example, a clinic would use text analytics for health on doctors' notes, not general NER. You can try these features in Foundry portal playgrounds.

concepts.heading: Azure Language or a Prompted Model
concepts.body: Many text tasks can also be done by a general-purpose model with a prompt such as 'Summarize this review and list the products mentioned'. The choice depends on what the app needs. Azure Language returns a fixed, documented structure every time, for example entities with categories and confidence scores, which code can parse reliably and which gives repeatable results. A prompted model is flexible: it can combine several tasks in one request, follow a custom style, answer follow-up questions, and needs no training data, but its output varies and must be checked. For example, a pipeline that must mask personal data before storing support tickets should call Azure Language PII detection and keep the redacted text, while a tool that drafts a friendly reply to each review suits a prompted model. They also work together: redact personal data with Azure Language first, then send only the redacted text to an agent or model.

concepts.heading: Speech to Text with Azure Speech
concepts.body: Azure Speech in Foundry Tools turns spoken audio into text. In the Speech SDK you create a SpeechConfig with your resource details, then a SpeechRecognizer. Single-shot recognition, `recognize_once_async()`, returns one utterance: it stops at a pause of silence or after at most 15 seconds of audio, so it suits short commands. For longer audio such as a meeting recording, use continuous recognition: call `start_continuous_recognition()`, collect the text from each recognized event, and call `stop_continuous_recognition()` when done. Set the speaker's language with `speech_recognition_language`, for example `de-DE` for German. When the language isn't known in advance but is one of a few candidates, use language identification instead of guessing. For example, an app that captures only the first sentence of a two-minute voicemail is using single-shot recognition where it needs continuous recognition. You can try speech to text on your own recordings in the Foundry portal before writing code.

concepts.heading: Text to Speech, SSML, and Speech Translation
concepts.body: Text to speech goes the other way. You set a voice with `speech_synthesis_voice_name` on the SpeechConfig and send text to a SpeechSynthesizer; an AudioOutputConfig sends the audio to the speaker or to a file. Neural voices are fluent in their own language and English, and multilingual voices cover more languages, so choose a voice that matches the text's language. For finer control, use Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML), an XML format that sets the voice, speaking rate, pitch, pronunciation and pauses; one SSML document can even switch between several voices, for example a narrator and a character, with break elements for pauses. Speech translation in Azure Speech translates live audio from a source language into one or more target languages, returning text, synthesized speech or both. For example, a lecture in Spanish can be shown as English and French captions at the same time, which is one source language and two target languages in a single translation request.

concepts.heading: Spoken Prompts: gpt-realtime and Voice Live
concepts.body: Sometimes the user speaks to a generative model and expects a spoken reply. The older approach chains three steps: speech to text, a text model, then text to speech. Speech-in, speech-out models remove the chain. A model such as gpt-realtime, called through the Realtime API, hears the audio prompt directly and can answer in audio with low latency; Learn recommends WebRTC for client apps and WebSocket for server-to-server work. The deployment must be an audio-capable model; a text-only deployment can't process speech. The Voice Live API goes further: it is fully managed, combining speech recognition, a generative model and text to speech in one interface, with features such as noise suppression, echo cancellation, interruption handling and end-of-turn detection, and you don't deploy the model yourself. Both are generally available. Choose the three-step pipeline when you need control over each step, such as SSML for the spoken output. A voice assistant that users interrupt mid-answer is a Voice Live scenario.

examPoints: A question about masking personal data, detecting a language or finding medical terms in text is testing Azure Language core capabilities: PII detection, language detection and text analytics for health.
A question that compares fixed, parseable output with flexible combined tasks is testing Azure Language versus a prompted model.

A question about transcribing long audio is testing continuous recognition, one about pauses or several voices is testing SSML, and one about a low-latency spoken assistant is testing gpt-realtime or Voice Live.

quiz.q: A hospital wants to pull medication names, dosages and diagnoses out of doctors' free-text notes and store them as structured data. Which Azure Language capability fits best?
choices: Text analytics for health, which extracts and labels medical information from clinical text
Key phrase extraction, which returns the main concepts of each note as a plain list of phrases
Language detection, which identifies the language of each note and returns a confidence score
Sentiment analysis, which labels each note as positive, negative or neutral for later review
quiz.explain: Text analytics for health is the core capability built for medical entities in clinical text. Choice B is tempting because key phrases pull out important terms, but they come back unlabeled, and key phrase extraction is a legacy capability.

quiz.q: A Python app transcribes recorded customer calls of about five minutes, but each transcript contains only the first sentence. The app calls recognize_once_async(). What should the developer change?
choices: Set speech_synthesis_voice_name to a multilingual voice so every speaker is recognized
Send the audio to a text-only chat deployment, which accepts audio prompts of any length
Use continuous recognition and collect the text from each recognized event until the end
Wrap the audio in an SSML document with break elements so the recognizer keeps listening
quiz.explain: Single-shot recognition returns one utterance, so long audio needs continuous recognition. Choice D is tempting because SSML handles pauses, but SSML controls text to speech output, not speech recognition.

days.recap: Azure Language core capabilities give fixed, structured text analysis while a prompted model gives flexible results; Azure Speech handles speech to text (single-shot or continuous), text to speech with voices and SSML, and speech translation, and gpt-realtime or Voice Live answer spoken prompts directly.

days.title: Vision Input with Multimodal Models

concepts.heading: Putting an Image in a Prompt
concepts.body: Vision-enabled models, such as the GPT-4.1, GPT-5 and GPT-4o series, are multimodal: they accept images as well as text and answer in text. They can recognize objects, shapes, colors and textures and read text inside an image. You send the image and the question together in one user message, as separate parts: a text part such as 'List the items on this receipt and the total' and an image part. With the Responses API the parts are `input_text` and `input_image`; with Chat Completions they are `text` and `image_url`. You can also set a detail level: low processes a small version of the image for faster replies and fewer tokens, high looks at detailed tiles for fine detail, and auto, the default, lets the model choose. For example, reading the small print on a photographed label calls for high detail. A system message still helps: Learn recommends making it specific to the task to avoid unhelpful replies.

concepts.heading: Image URL or Base64 Data
concepts.body: There are two common ways to supply the image. A URL works when the image is publicly reachable over HTTP or HTTPS, because the service fetches the image itself from Microsoft's managed infrastructure. That is also why private endpoints, firewall-restricted storage and VNet-only URLs fail even inside your own network: the fetch doesn't come from your network. For local files or private images, read the file, encode it as base64 and send it as a data URL such as `data:image/jpeg;base64,...` in the same image part. The Responses API can also take a file ID created with the Files API. Supported formats include JPEG, PNG, WEBP and GIF (first frame only). For example, a phone app that photographs a meter reading sends the photo as base64, while a website that already hosts product photos publicly can pass their URLs. If an image 'isn't processed', check that the URL is public or the base64 encoding is correct.

concepts.heading: What Vision Models Do Well and Their Limits
concepts.body: Vision models are strong at describing scenes, answering questions about photos, explaining charts and screenshots in plain language, and reading printed text in a picture. Learn also lists limits you should know. They aren't suitable for specialized medical images such as CT scans and shouldn't be used for medical advice. They can give approximate counts of objects, so don't rely on them alone where exact numbers matter. They struggle with precise spatial localization, such as identifying chess positions, and with rotated or upside-down text, panoramic and fisheye images, and charts whose lines differ only by color or style. Small text should be enlarged, by a closer shot or a crop, without cutting off important details. The model sees pixels and your prompt only: it doesn't read file names or metadata, so put any context in the text part. For example, 'This is a photo of a kitchen fuse box; which switch is off?' beats 'What is in this image?'.

concepts.heading: Choosing and Calling a Vision-Capable Deployment
concepts.body: Not every deployment can see. Learn lists which model families are vision-enabled, and only a deployment of one of them will process the image part. The usual path is: deploy the model, test image prompts in the chat playground by attaching an image, then copy the sample from the Code tab into your app. A minimal client needs three values: the endpoint, a credential (Microsoft Entra ID preferred, or a key kept out of the code) and the deployment name. In code the model parameter is the deployment name you chose, not the catalog name, so a deployment called vision-prod is called as vision-prod even if the model is gpt-4.1. Set an output limit with max_tokens or max_completion_tokens; if finish_reason is length, raise it. Guardrails check image inputs too, across categories such as hate, sexual content, violence and self-harm. For example, a 'deployment not found' error usually means the code used the model name.

concepts.heading: Retiring Vision Services and Where to Move
concepts.body: Two older Azure Vision services are on their way out, and the exam expects you not to pick them for new work. The Image Analysis API, versions 3.2 and 4.0, retires on September 25, 2028, for cloud APIs and for connected and disconnected containers; after that date calls fail. Azure Custom Vision is supported until the same date. Learn's migration guide points to alternatives by scenario: GPT models in Foundry or Azure Content Understanding for captions, tags and other image understanding; Azure Document Intelligence for OCR of text in images; the Face API for face detection; multimodal embedding models in Foundry for image search; and for custom image classification, Azure Content Understanding or Azure Machine Learning AutoML. For example, a new app that must describe user photos and answer open questions about them should use a vision-enabled model, not Image Analysis. If a stem offers a retiring service as the new design, treat it as a distractor.

examPoints: A question about sending a private or local image to a model is testing base64 data URLs, while one about a hosted public image is testing image URLs.
A question about medical scans, exact object counts or precise positions is testing the documented limits of vision models.
A question that offers Image Analysis or Custom Vision for a new app is testing the September 25, 2028 retirement; choose a vision-enabled model in Foundry or Content Understanding instead.

quiz.q: A company's app sends photos stored in a storage account that is reachable only through a private endpoint. The vision model reports that it can't access the image URL. What should the developer do?
choices: Add the storage account's private endpoint to the model deployment's guardrail settings
Put the full image URL in the system message instead of in the image part of the request
Switch to a deployment with a larger context window so the model can download the image
Read each image in the app and send it as base64 data in the image part of the message
quiz.explain: The service fetches image URLs from Microsoft's infrastructure, not from inside the network, so private images must be sent as base64 data. Choice B is tempting because it changes where the URL appears, but the model would still be unable to fetch the private image.

quiz.q: A warehouse app needs the exact number of boxes on each pallet for billing. A developer suggests asking a vision-enabled model to count the boxes in a photo. What is the main concern?
choices: Vision models only accept charts and screenshots, so they can't analyze photos of pallets
Vision models must use the low detail setting, which hides boxes at the edge of the photo
Vision models may give only approximate counts, too rough to rely on alone for billing
Vision models read only file names and metadata, so the boxes in the picture are never seen
quiz.explain: Learn lists counting as a limit: the model may give approximate counts. Choice B is tempting because detail affects accuracy, but low is not required; the default is auto, and high detail still doesn't make counts exact.

days.recap: A vision-enabled deployment answers questions about images sent as public URLs or base64 data in the same user message as the text, works best with clear instructions and enlarged small text, has documented limits such as medical images and counting, and replaces the Image Analysis and Custom Vision services that retire on September 25, 2028.

days.title: Image Generation

concepts.heading: GPT-Image Models in Foundry
concepts.body: Image generation models turn a text prompt, and optionally input images, into new images. In Foundry these are the GPT-image series. Their status matters on the exam. GPT-image-2 is generally available and suits high-resolution output, improved editing and many aspect ratios. GPT-image-1, GPT-image-1-mini and GPT-image-1.5 are limited access previews that need an approved application. The older dall-e-3 model was retired on March 4, 2026; existing deployments no longer work, and Learn says to use a GPT-image series model instead. Keep the direction straight: vision-enabled chat models turn images into text, while GPT-image models turn text into images. For example, a marketing team that wants new banner pictures from a description deploys a GPT-image model; a team that wants descriptions of existing photos deploys a vision-enabled chat model. If an exam stem still mentions DALL-E, it is testing whether you know it is retired.

concepts.heading: Writing Image Prompts and Using the Images Playground
concepts.body: Learn's advice for image prompts is short: describe the content you want to see and the visual style. Content covers the subject, setting and composition, such as 'a red bicycle leaning on a stone wall in a quiet village street, morning light'. Style covers how it should look, such as 'watercolor', 'flat vector illustration' or 'photorealistic', plus colors and mood. A vague prompt like 'a nice bike' leaves the model to guess. The easiest place to experiment is the images playground in the Foundry portal: when you open the playground for an image model, Foundry shows the images experience, where you type a prompt, adjust settings such as size and quality, and generate. It also supports inpainting and comparing models. When the result is right, select View code to get a Python or cURL sample prefilled with your settings, and reuse it in your app. On the exam, 'try prompts without code, then move to an app' points to the images playground and View code.

concepts.heading: Quality, Size, and Speed
